newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND MOURNS FLOOD DEAD AND BRACES FOR MORE RAIN.
newsitem.headline: POLAND MOURNS FLOOD DEAD AND BRACES FOR MORE RAIN.

text.p: The traumatised people of southwest Poland, reeling from the worst flood disaster in centuries, braced themselves on Friday to face a new deluge as forecasters predicted heavy rain.
Poland was to hold a national day of mourning, with flags lowered, to grieve over the 11-day calamity that has already taken 48 lives and devastated thousands of others.
Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz sounded the alarm to an emergency session of parliament meeting on Thursday to pass bills easing relief efforts.

In the Czech Republic, at least 46 people have been killed in the worst flooding within the region for a century. The country was braced for more misery as weathermen forecast renewed heavy rain at the weekend.
The Czech Weather Service said heavy rain was expected to sweep in from Austria and head for the flood-hit east Bohemia and Moravia regions.
Outlining the situation in Poland, Cimoszewicz said forecasters expected downpours in the night and later on terrain so water-logged it could absorb little more.
"This will mean more very serious rains and a build up of water in conditions worse than some days ago...so unfortunately we must expect another wave of floods," he said.
"I appeal to residents of (threatened) areas, please, without panic, quietly prepare for what may happen," he said.
Learning lessons from the initial catastrophe, the government deployed more than 20,000 troops to help with flood defences and set up a special communications network.
Financial markets also waited nervously.

The Polish zloty, which took a battering on Tuesday, got another jolt after the prime minister's announcement and dropped one percent. The share market, more resilient as few major companies have been hard-hit, was also jittery.

The country's establishment and foreign investors were wondering what the catastrophe would mean for Poland's economic stability especially after the government won parliament's approval for greater borrowing.

Among bills passed by the lower house were a relaxation of limits in this year's budget to give room for 2.5 billion zlotys ($714 million) of extra government borrowing from the central bank and a $300 million soft loan from the World Bank.

But high finance was far from the minds of exhausted people who faced a repeat of the nightmare that swamped more than 4,000 sq km of land and 970 towns and villages, 176 of which remained flooded on Thursday.
The current floods starting early last week inundated the south and then sent great swells northwards along the Wisla and Odra rivers, drowning the city streets of Wroclaw and Opole.
The 650,000 residents of Wroclaw, many of whom had worked day and night to build barriers that saved much of the historic city centre at the weekend, were urged to reinforce them.
Even as the new rain loomed, the earlier Odra wave was marching towards the German border, prompting evacuations in parts of the Polish frontier town of Slubice.
Opposition parliamentarians, critical of the government's crisis management and scenting blood before elections on September 21, renewed their attacks on Thursday.
They tried to reject the ex-communist-led government's report justifying its actions, but lost the vote in parliament.
Later opposition deputies approached President Aleksander Kwasniewski to ask him to declare a state of emergency -- a move which the prime minister says is unnecessary.
The president backed Cimoszewicz, especially as the current law on states of emergency involves suspending political parties, banning public assemblies and would mean delaying the polls.
But Kwasniewski proposed an amended law, without such draconian measures, so it could be used later if necessary. Parliament was still examining it late on Thursday.
